# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions is the obvious last decision before my study goes out to strangers, right after the pilot.
screens.why2: The question itself is plain, but the hint's 'needs Keel's credits' and 'links go out as text' takes a second read, because it doesn't say whether the AI interviewer speaks aloud or types, and that matters most for my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents.
screens.why3: Deciding how my own study is run is my call and something I know.
screens.why4: Locking a preselected interviewer face works, but the choice doesn't show whether the AI interviewer is captioned or text-only, and for deaf and hard-of-hearing adults a voice-only interviewer would be the wrong answer missing a clear alternative.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is changed here; it only sets how the questions reach people.
screens.instead: Who asks the questions? AI interviewer (spoken with live captions, needs Keel credits) / Text-only link they read and answer (free) -- your respondents are deaf or hard of hearing, so pick a mode they can follow.

screens.why1: Choosing how respondents answer is the obvious last step before sending, right after who asks the questions.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'More than 90% in loud places down to 5 dB.Hear it' runs a vague accuracy claim into a link label; I know dB from hearing tech, yet I still have to reread it to work out that it means signal-to-noise.
screens.why3: I know my respondents are deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, so I can answer this straight away: they need to read the questions, not hear them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete, but the AI option's text is garbled and never says whether the spoken questions are also captioned, which decides whether my respondents can use it at all.
screens.why5: My pick, 'Text only', is shown exactly as I chose it, and nothing of my study is changed.
screens.instead: How should they answer? AI interviewer (asks each question aloud with on-screen captions; they talk or tap; needs Keel's credits) / Text only (they read each question and tap) / Let them choose (needs Keel's credits). Note: if your respondents are deaf or hard of hearing, text only or captions are needed.

screens.why1: Once I've chosen how they answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: "Someone I know" is plain, but "People from a dataset ... on Contacts" makes me stop: I can't tell if Contacts means my phone's contacts or a Keel page, and "dataset" isn't how I'd talk about deaf and hard-of-hearing people I'd reach.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I'd send this to: TranscribeGlass users, waitlist people and the HoH folks I've met over the years, each by name.
screens.why4: The two options are distinct and my pick is there, but the second is in Keel's words rather than mine, and there's no option for an open link I could post in a hearing-loss group or forum.
screens.why5: This screen is only about sending, and nothing I typed about AirCaps is changed here.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know, by name (you send each link) / People Keel found for me (from my Contacts list in Keel) / An open link I post myself (a group, forum or newsletter)

screens.why1: As the first screen it plainly checks whether I'm someone this study is about, and I am, since I talk with hearing people at work and in shops all the time.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is our own word for them, so I understand it on first reading or hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly how often I talk with hearing people, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it completely, and a screener gate needs no escape option.
screens.why5: Nothing about any product or company reaches me, and the wording is the way deaf people talk about this.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options that are easy to hold when heard once, though "I'll read 2 options" is a little stiff for just yes or no.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, asking about a hard conversation in the last week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Every word is plain to me, and "too fast or noisy" is exactly how those conversations go wrong, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know whether I lost track of someone at work, in a shop or at dinner this week, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the two chips are odd: "I can't recall one particular face-to-face conversation" is a long sentence that doesn't fit a yes-or-no about the week, and "I'd rather not say" is a second escape on a gate that should have none.
screens.why5: Nothing of anyone's product or plan reaches me, only my own situation in words I would use.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is one short question ending "Yes or no.", easy to hear once and answer, and the gate correctly speaks no escape.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you struggle to follow a face-to-face conversation with hearing people because it was too fast or too noisy? Yes / No (no chips)

screens.why1: After two questions about struggling to follow fast or noisy talk, showing me the idea at the start of part 2 makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: Captions, glasses and keeping eye contact are words I live with, so I get it on one read.
screens.why3: It's set in exactly the moment I deal with every week, a fast or noisy conversation with hearing people, so I can picture it in my own life.
screens.why4: It's a card to read with no options or box.
screens.why5: The product is shown on purpose as an idea card, and nothing else of the founder's plans or labels for people comes through in odd words.
screens.why6: The middle sentence runs past twenty words and carries two clauses, and 'the lightweight glasses' sounds like glasses I should already know about, so said once it takes some holding.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps. When a conversation is too fast or too noisy, you wear light glasses. Live captions of what people around you say appear in the lens. The people building it believe you could read the words and still keep eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card it makes sense to ask whether the idea would have fitted my last conversation with hearing people.
screens.why2: "Fitted the way things were set up for you" makes me read it twice -- set up how, the room, my hearing aids, the people, my interpreter? -- and I would not say it that way.
screens.why3: I can picture my last conversation, but "Imagine AirCaps" tells me nothing about what it is, so I would partly be guessing whether it would have fitted.
screens.why4: Yes, Mostly, Partly, No are distinct and cover it, and "I can't tell" fits someone who is unsure.
screens.why5: The product name AirCaps reaches me with nothing in my words about what it does, so it reads as the company's label rather than something I know.
screens.why6: It is short and the four options say well, but "the way things were set up for you" is a vague mouthful heard once, and hearing it aloud is the hard part for me anyway.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Could you have used live captions on glasses there without anything getting in the way? Yes; Mostly; Partly; or No. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after asking if it would have fitted my last conversation, asking whether it would have made things better is the natural next question.
screens.why2: The question itself is plain, but 'AirCaps' is just a name to me and the second option reads like a different kind of answer, so I'd have to read the list twice.
screens.why3: I can picture my last noisy conversation, but I only know AirCaps from the card, so I'd be partly guessing how it would have gone.
screens.why4: 'Following more without asking anyone to repeat' is a reason rather than a level and overlaps with 'It would have made things better', so the options are not distinct, though the escape 'I can't tell' fits.
screens.why5: The idea card is meant to show me AirCaps, but the line about not asking anyone to repeat sounds like the company's selling point slipped in as an answer.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, but hearing a benefit phrase in the middle of a better / same / worse list is a mouthful that breaks the pattern I'm holding.
screens.instead: Would AirCaps have made that conversation easier to follow, or not? Much easier; A bit easier; No different; Harder. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: After hearing what AirCaps is and whether it would help, it makes sense to ask whether I would actually wear the glasses in my conversations.
screens.why2: Wearing glasses paired to my phone during a conversation is plain to me, and I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know whether I would put on captioning glasses when I'm talking with hearing people, from how I already handle those conversations.
screens.why4: The scale is lopsided: the second yes adds a condition while the other options are just yes, probably not and no, so there is no plain probably-yes and the hedges don't mirror each other.
screens.why5: AirCaps was shown to me on purpose on the idea card, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms comes through.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options and one escape said last, so I can hold it after hearing it once.
screens.instead: AirCaps means wearing the glasses, paired to your phone, during conversations. Would you do that, or not? Yes; Probably yes; Probably not; or No. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: After I've said whether I'd wear the glasses, asking what would make it worth it is a natural last question.
screens.why2: "It" is vague on first hearing, since I can't tell if it means the glasses, the cost, or the hassle of pairing to my phone, so I'd pause before answering.
screens.why3: I know what I'd need to keep up in a noisy restaurant or a fast meeting, so I can answer this from my own life.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in with no options.
screens.why5: "Clearly worth it" sounds like a sales or pricing pitch rather than how I'd talk about following a conversation, though nothing new about the product leaks in.
screens.why6: It's one short question with no list, slash or parenthesis, so I'd hear it once and could answer.
screens.instead: What would the glasses need to do for you to wear them in your next conversation with hearing people?
